jobs.title: National Anticipatory Action Manager
jobs.description:
DRC Uganda is currently looking for a highly qualified and motivated individual to join our dynamic team as National Anticipatory Action Manager.

**The overall purpose of the role:**

The National Anticipatory Action Manager will lead the national portion of the global Anticipatory Humanitarian Action for Displacement (AHEAD) project implemented across seven countries globally, funded by the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The project will develop anticipatory action (AA) data models and approaches using local and global data for local-level analysis to help inform humanitarian actors’ decisions when deploying humanitarian assistance and to enable timelier, more dignified, efficient and sustainable assistance. He/she will also be responsible for technical coordination and representation in coordination forums in Uganda and support the Country Office with technical backstopping when necessary.

**Your main duties and responsibilities will be:**

**Management and Coordination:**

- Ensure timely and quality deliverables and spending of the AHEAD project.
- Ensure effecitve, respectful coordination with communities and partners that are part of the project’s implementation.
- Ensure effective Project Cycle Management (PCM).
- Support DRC Uganda’s Anticipatory Action (AA) sector, ensuring alignment with DRC’s global strategy and the country’s specific needs;
- Coordinate with regional and global teams to ensure effective integration of anticipatory action activities into overall program strategies;
- Facilitate awareness-raising and collaboration across sectors and with key stakeholders, including government agencies, local partners, and UN agencies
- Provide effective leadership to the AHEAD team in Uganda and to the project partners.
- Lead the AHEAD Uganda advocacy strategy so that displacement forecasting is built into national and district early warning, preparedness and disaster risk financing systems.
- Engage the Office of the Prime Minister (Department of Relief, Disaster Preparedness and Management), Conflict Early Warning and Early Response Unit (CEWERU), National Emergency Coordination and Operations Centre (NECOC), Uganda National Meteorological Authority (UNMA) and district disaster management committees to show how displacement forecasts can inform triggers, contingency plans and early action decisions.
- Promote the use of displacement forecasts and conflict and protection risk indicators alongside climate hazard data in national anticipatory action frameworks, protocols and technical working groups.
- Represent DRC in national platforms and within the AA Technical Working Group (TWG), and push for displacement- and conflict-sensitive AA and for more locally led approaches
- Manage the project budget: track spending against plans, forecast burn rates, and flag and resolve over- or under-spending in good time
- Ensure compliance with donor regulations, DRC procedures and audit requirements across DRC and partner implementation.
- Lead donor reporting and maintain good relationships with the donor, including preparing amendments or no-cost extensions where needed.
- Line-manage, and assess the performance of AHEAD team members, and identify and support their learning and development needs.

**Partnership management**

- Manage day-to-day relationships with implementing partners, including regular check-ins, joint work planning and clear communication on roles, timelines and expectations.
- Carry out partner capacity assessments and develop and follow up on capacity-strengthening plans. These should cover AA concepts, trigger monitoring, early action implementation, financial management, compliance, safeguarding and MEAL.
- Deliver or coordinate training, mentoring and on-the-job coaching for partner staff and local structures (e.g. district committees, community monitors).
- Monitor partner performance on activities, spending and reporting through field visits, review meetings and spot checks, and follow up on corrective actions.
- Review partner narrative and financial reports for quality, accuracy and compliance with DRC and donor requirements.
- Support partners in psreparing and running activations, including readiness checks, pre-positioning, beneficiary targeting and post-activation reviews.
- Manage partnership agreements in line with DRC partnership policy, from due diligence and agreement development to amendments and close-out.
- Promote equitable partnerships and localisation, including partner participation in decisions, visibility, and access to learning and advocacy spaces.

**Implementation and Technical Support of AHEAD:**

- Lead the development and implementation of anticipatory action plans, including leading the co-design of readiness and anticipatory actions, trigger mechanisms, and evidence generation frameworks, following a participatory, bottom-up design process;
- Oversee trigger monitoring and early warning analysis, and coordinate activation decisions and the timely release of pre-arranged funds.
- Lead the anticipatory action systems building, including strengthening of early warning systems, trigger development, and development of anticipatory action plans in close collaboration with duty bearers and in-country partners, ensuring they meet DRC’s standards and principles;
- Identify funding opportunities and contribute to concept notes and proposals to scale up or continue AA work in Uganda and the region.

**Data, Analysis, and Learning:**

- Model use, refinement and dissemination: Work with Headquarter's (HQ’s) Evidence, Knowledge, and Learning (EKL) team to ensure that data and displacement forecasting models are effectively used for anticipatory action; support DRC’s global and regional analysts (via coordination of AHEAD’s community protection monitoring) to monitor and analyze data related to disaster risks and displacement, ensuring that forecasts and triggers are aligned with the evolving needs on the ground;
- MEAL: Support the MEAL Assistant as appropriate in capturing and disseminate lessons learned from anticipatory action projects, contributing to global, regional and national knowledge-sharing and advocacy efforts.
- Oversee the MEAL framework, including baselines, monitoring of early actions, post-activation reviews and evaluation of anticipatory action effectiveness (timeliness, avoided losses).
- Document and share lessons learned and good practice with country, regional and global teams and external stakeholders.

**Reporting and Communication:**

• Ensure timely and high-quality reporting on project activities, in line with donor and organizational requirements; maintain strong communication with country focal points to track progress, share updates, and resolve challenges in implementation; provide regular technical support and guidance to local staff and stakeholders, ensuring clear understanding and commitment to AA objectives.

About you

- To be successful in this role, you must have at least 5 years of international experience in disaster risk management or anticipatory action programming, preferably in conflict-affected regions. Moreover, we also expect the following.

*Required*

- Bachelor’s degree in Political Science, Social Sciences, Peacebuilding, or similar relevant field, or significant additional demonstrable past professional experience gained through fieldwork
- Proven track record of efective and timely project management.
- Strong knowledge of PCM.
- Proven track record of designing and implementing anticipatory action projects, including development of triggers and anticipatory action planning.
- Strong understanding of data-driven decision-making, with experience with displacement forecasting models and early warning systems being a strong asset.
- Excellent stakeholder coordination skills, with an ability to navigate diverse stakeholder groups and drive joint progress to achieve common goals.
- Excellent partner management and communication skills.
- Familiarity with conflict-sensitive programming and the impacts of displacement on vulnerable populations.
- Ability and willingness to travel, including to remote or conflict-affected areas, up to 35% of the time.
- Excellent interpersonal, communication, and coordination skills, with the ability to work across multiple teams and with diverse stakeholders.

*Desirable*

- Experience with programming related to climate resilience, preparedness, and conflict sensitivity.
- Demonstrated ability to innovate and take a flexible, problem-solving approach in complex humanitarian environments.
- Strong project management skills and experience with donor reporting and proposal writing.
- Familiarity with humanitarian coordination mechanisms and key international standards

In this position, you are expected to demonstrate DRC’s five core competencies:

**Striving for excellence**: You focus on reaching results while ensuring an efficient process.

**Collaborating**: You involve relevant parties and encourage feedback.

**Taking the lead**: You take ownership and initiative while aiming for innovation.

**Communicating:** You listen and speak effectively and honestly.

**Demonstrating integrity**: You uphold and promote the highest standards of ethical and professional conduct in relation to our values and Code of Conduct, including safeguarding against sexual exploitation, abuse and harassment.

We offer

- Contract length: 12 months
- Band: M F2
- Designation of Duty Station: Arua
- Start date: January 2027

Salary and conditions will be in accordance with Danish Refugee Council’s Terms of Employment for national employees; please refer to [our website](https://drc.ngo/about-drc/vacancies).

DEPARTMENT & TEAM PURPOSE:
To act with poor people as a force for change in addressing the causes of poverty, suffering and injustice and alleviating their symptoms.
Responsible for implementing and maintaining Oxfam and donor logistics and procurement procedures and effective logistics management support to partners.

JOB PURPOSE:
To secure a perfect procurement process in the country office according to Oxfam policies and procedures mainly for high level of thresholds and address the properly related reports.
Answer the received procurement requests in the best manner within the appropriate timeline according to Oxfam regulation.
Maintain good relationships with suppliers and other stakeholders by following Oxfam values.

KEY RESPONSIBILITIES
Procurement:
•Perform various actions related to procurement, including but not limited to flash quotations, preparing official requests for quotation, bids analysis, purchase orders, receive goods and issue payments.
•Participate in preparations for matters related to tenders, such as, but not limited to: invitation to tenders, advertisements, amendments and advertising in accordance to standards
•Provide assistance in the finalization of purchase orders as per specifications and issue contracts,
•annexes, and amendments for approvals by the authorized official.
•Support in the preparation of framework agreements with selected suppliers when necessary
•Support hubs with various requests

•Monitor requisitions spending and make sure all expenditures are pre-authorized.
•Produce accurate contracts, reflecting winner information and BoCs conditions.

Logistics:

•Take responsibility for ensuring the logistics activities in Oxfam in the Country and hubs offices are carried out in accordance with the authority of the logistics.
Assets and Equipment:

•Contribute to ensuring all assets and Oxfam properties are maintained to a good working order and appropriate standard.
•Ensure that any storage facilities and/or warehouses are adequately maintained and managed, including the protection of stored goods
•Support in checking all records related to vehicle timetables, log sheets, vehicle servicing history, accident/incident reports are up to date, etc.

Warehousing and Transportation:
Ensure timely movement of the goods to/from warehouse by:

•Attend and effectively participate in the logistics cluster meetings whenever designated to maintain working relationships
•Prepare, follow on facilitation letters required for transportation as per local legislations.

General:

•Recommend and advise on any improvement or changes to these procedures as a means of further strengthening best practices adapted to the local context.
•Responsible for maintaining good and professional relations and establishing good contacts with vendor-suppliers, other humanitarian actors, and government departments that relate to logistics.
•Ensure effective supply chain mechanisms are in place to contribute to the successful implementation of the Oxfam GB plans in Syria in coordination with the different internal and external stakeholders.
Perform any other tasks as assigned by the line manager.

ESSENTIAL:
•Sound judgement
•Listening
•Self-Awareness
• Decisiveness
•Self-Awareness

In addition:
•University Degree – relevant to the position is preferable.

•Competency in use of relevant technology systems (MS Office suite skills). Financial management ability and value for money achievement are essential
•Very good analytical thinking and ability to take sound judgements/decisions and be able to work independently.
•Fluency in Arabic and English (written and verbal)
•Diplomacy, tact, and negotiating skills.

Desirable:
•Team-working skills.
•Flexibility under pressure and in response to changing needs.
•Attention to detail and excellent numeracy.
•Good interpersonal and communication skills
•Ability to pro-actively adapt and improve standards and working practices, and continually seek out the most efficient use of resources

Program Support Manager - Secondment to the Justice Centre for Legal Aid (JCLA)
jobs.description:
**What we are looking for**

Are you an experienced humanitarian professional with a strong track record in donor engagement and grants management, particularly in recovery, humanitarian, or conflict-affected settings? We're looking for someone who understands the Jordanian context, has solid knowledge of National NGO operations and humanitarian sector dynamics, and ideally brings experience working with local and national civil society organizations (CSOs).

Experience in MEAL (Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability, and Learning) approaches and systems strengthening is highly desirable, as these areas are central to the role.

We're especially interested in candidates with a strategic mindset and proven expertise in strengthening institutional systems on grants management, fundraising and MEAL.

If you're passionate about strengthening organizational capacity, developing people and teams, and driving meaningful impact, this could be an excellent opportunity to take your career to the next level.

**Applicants must be legally eligible to work in Amman Jordan, We are unable to provide work permits or visa sponsorships for this position.**

**What you will do**

The Programme Support Manager will be full-time seconded to NRC’s strategic partner, the Justice Centre for Legal Aid (JCLA) contributing e to achieve programme quality and accountability by strengthening overall system and managements of JCLA’s grants and MEAL functions and leading the review and improvement of internal processes and procedures.

The Programme Support Manager is responsible for leading the fundraising strategy by providing insight on funding trends, supporting donor engagement, ensuring donor compliance, leading on the development of high quality and timely proposals and reports and other external products, as well as ensuring robust MEAL systems and processes are in place to promote evidence-based decision making, project performance, and internal management.

Key responsibilities:

- **Grant Management and Compliance**: Ensure compliance with NRC and JCLA policies, donor regulations, grant agreements, and reporting requirements while strengthening internal grant management systems and processes.
- **Fundraising and Business Development**: Support the development and implementation of fundraising strategies, donor engagement, preparation and submission of high-quality concept notes, proposals, budgets, and funding applications, in close collaboration with JCLA’s Executive Director.
- **Programme Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability and Learning (MEAL)**: Provide technical oversight and continuous improvement of MEAL systems, complaint feedback mechanisms (CFM), data analysis, and learning processes to support strategic and programme decision-making.
- **Project Cycle Management and Capacity Building**: Lead and strengthen Project Cycle Management (PCM) processes across all stages, including staff training, technical guidance, proposal development, reporting, and integration of cross-cutting programme elements.
- **Management, Coordination and Representation**: Manage and support staff performance and development, coordinate with NRC and external stakeholders, and represent JCLA with partners and donors as delegated by leadership.

**What you will bring**

- Five years of demonstrated relevant and related experience in a similar working experience in a humanitarian/recovery context with Knowledge of the Jordan context, NGO operations and the dynamics of the humanitarian sector, preferably with a working experience with local and national CSOs.
- Experience working in complex environments and with Displacement affected people.
- Experience of donor relations and grants management. Proven skills and experience in report and proposal development and working with multiple donors and working with budgets.
- Experience in design, implementation, and oversight of monitoring and evaluation with advanced experience in qualitative and quantitative data analysis and tools.
- Good personal organizational skills, interpersonal skills, team management, including time management, and ability to meet deadlines and work under pressure.
- Demonstrated experience of contributing to positive organizational change.
- Excellent written and oral communication skills in English and Arabic.
- Above average computer skills, particularly in Microsoft Windows Word and Excel.

Please download[ the detailed job description](https://norwegianrefugeecouncil.sharepoint.com/:w:/s/JDsforNRCPeople/IQALzwQyzc2USbBDiVJU-hvrATBWVwrB3o_NuII2shAVHBU?e=Wmbkwq) to learn more about the position.

**What we offer**

- Duty station: Amman, Jordan
- Fixed term contract: 12 months national contract, renewable based on performance and availability of funding
- Travel: Up to 5%
- Salary/benefits: Grade 9 on NRC's grading structure.
- NRC is an equal opportunities employer. We are committed to diversity without distinction to age, gender, religion, ethnicity, nationality, and physical ability.
- We think outside the box, encourage ideas, and give responsibility to all employees at all levels. You will have many opportunities to be heard and take the initiative.

[Find out more about the benefits of working for NRC](https://www.nrc.no/career/what-we-offer/)

Important information about the application process

- We invite applications from qualified candidates matching the profile. Applicants must be legally eligible to work in Amman Jordan, We are unable to provide work permits or visa sponsorships for this position.
- Please ensure you attach copies of your academic and professional certificates.
- To apply as an internal candidate, log in with your official email address or click on Opportunity Marketplace.
- When creating your profile, include your full name as given on your passport. Complete all the system-required fields for experience, employment history and education.
- Submit your application and CV in English, taking care to attach your latest CV.
- Applications that do not meet the minimum standards in terms of experience or qualifications will generally not be considered. Unsolicited applications not related to this specific job advertisement will not be considered.
- Only shortlisted candidates will be contacted. We receive many applicants for each vacant position.

**Why NRC?**

The Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) is an independent humanitarian organisation helping people forced to flee. Our 15,000 staff work in crises across 40 countries, providing life-saving and long-term assistance to millions of people every year.

[Watch this short video](https://vimeo.com/736782633) to see NRC in action.

We are looking for people who are passionate about helping refugees and people forced to flee. Are you one of those people? If you are, NRC offers you the opportunity to:

- do demanding and professional work, often in challenging contexts
- join a work culture that empowers every employee to share ideas and take responsibility
- be part of a welcoming and supportive community committed to human dignity

**Why JCLA?**

The Justice Centre for Legal Aid (JCLA) is a Jordanian not-for-profit legal aid organisation promoting legal empowerment. JCLA was founded in 2008 on the belief that legal protection should be a basic right accessible by all, regardless of their economic vulnerability. Our intervention relies on three main pillars: Prevention through legal awareness, Response through legal services and Advocacy for institutional change.

[Learn more about NRC Jordan](https://www.nrc.no/countries/middle-east/jordan)

jobs.title: HRO - Human Resources Officer Operation Cell 4 (M/F)
jobs.description:
## **Position Context:**

The HRO position is fully integrated into the operational Cell, a multidisciplinary team of around ten people supporting field missions and operations. The cell currently coordinates three countries (Afghanistan, Haiti, Nigeria), representing nearly 2,500 national colleagues and approximately 120 international staff. The portfolio may evolve over time.

Within this cell, the HR Manager works in body partnership with another HR officer. This organization aims to foster professional exchange, knowledge sharing, and joint reflection on key HR issues. The two managers share leadership of the countries within the portfolio as well as certain cross-functional files, while maintaining a sufficiently in-depth understanding of all contexts to ensure continuity of activities during absences, leave, or field visits by their counterpart.

The position holder acts as an HR partner for operations by providing advice, support, and expertise to field and coordination teams. He/she also contributes to the continuous improvement of HR practices within the cell and actively participates in cross-functional discussions conducted with other departments.

The position requires an excellent knowledge of colleagues at headquarters as well as of the OCP international staff pool. This detailed understanding of profiles, competencies, and career paths is essential to support missions in identifying and mobilizing resources adapted to their needs.

**Current Challenges of the Position:**

We are looking for someone with a strong interest in social dialogue issues and the ways in which it can be organized within MSF intervention contexts.

The position also involves a strong commitment to duty of care, staff solidarity, and the implementation and monitoring of support mechanisms and associated good practices.

Promoting a safe and respectful work environment is also a key responsibility. The HR Manager contributes to the dissemination of safeguarding principles, awareness raising among project and coordination teams, the establishment of appropriate reporting mechanisms, and the diligent handling of alerts, in close collaboration with the relevant specialist teams.

Particular attention is paid to supporting international staff throughout their professional pathway, notably through the organization and quality of mission departure and return debriefings.

Finally, the position offers the opportunity to contribute to high-impact cross-functional HR files linked to the cell's and organization's strategic priorities. This dimension represents an important lever for professional development and provides the opportunity to actively contribute to the evolution of MSF's HR policies and practices.

## **Responsibilities:**

Under the responsibility of the Cell Manager and with a functional reporting line to the Head of the Operational HR, the Operational HR officer is the strategic HR partner of the cell. He/she ensures, within the countries under his/her responsibility, the quality and consistency of the HR response, its adaptation to operational realities, and its contribution to mission impact. He/she supports operations in understanding human issues, identifying HR needs, and defining appropriate responses. He/she contributes to operational management through contextual analysis, advice to operational stakeholders, and leadership of the HR function within his/her scope. He/she ensures the mobilization of relevant expertise, the clarification of programme needs, and the consistency of the responses provided.

Your main activities, as a member of the Cell HR team, are as follows:

**1. Lead the HR contribution to operations management** o Participate in defining objectives and developing operational strategies for the cell’s programmes. o Bring an HR perspective to decisions, anticipate human and capacity risks, and alert the cell to these risks. o Inform decision-making and contribute to the cell’s cross-functional projects by providing an HR perspective, facilitating implementation, and contributing to prioritization. o Contribute to the cell’s strategic reflections by providing analysis of human issues, organizational capacities, and their operational consequences.

**2. Lead the HR strategy within the assigned scope** o Assess HR dynamics in the countries under his/her responsibility and contribute to the cell’s strategic reflections. o Coordinate with counterparts from other Operational Centres (OCs) on the implementation of intersectional HR policies within the scope. o Contribute to anticipating HR needs and forecasting the resources required within the scope.

**3. Identify needs and direct them to the appropriate stakeholder** o Help programmes define the actual HR need, which is not always the one initially expressed, and direct it towards the appropriate expertise or lever. o Ensure the mobilization of appropriate expertise and the proper coordination of interventions with programme needs. o Support functional managers and coordination teams in decision-making and in the implementation of HR policies, procedures, and tools.

**4. Ensure the application and adaptation of HR frameworks** o Ensure the dissemination and compliance with HR policies and procedures within the scope, relying on headquarters expertise and technical coordination. o Be responsible for their implementation and adaptation at country level, while respecting common principles. o Advise the Cell Manager on exceptions when operational constraints require them, seek arbitration when necessary, and ensure the follow-up and capitalization of approved exceptions.

**5. Support and lead the team and coordinations** o Define the cell’s HR priorities, manage the HR team, foster skills development, and strengthen team cohesion. o Ensure a coherent distribution of responsibilities, activities, and workload within the HR team. o Support HR coordinations in the countries under responsibility, while respecting the leadership they exercise within their own scope, by providing headquarters perspective and comparative insight across multiple contexts. o Promote a shared analysis of HR challenges and support the critical reflection necessary for complex decisions.

**6. Contribute to HR developments and transformations** o Contribute to HR transformation initiatives affecting the scope and promote ownership by the teams concerned. o Escalate the development needs arising from the evolution of the countries under responsibility and contribute to designing appropriate responses.

**7. Monitor, analyse and report** o Ensure the collection of management information and HR reporting within the scope. o Analyse HR issues specific to the countries under responsibility and communicate them to the Head of the Operational HR Scope. o Contribute to identifying, planning, and monitoring the resources necessary for implementing HR priorities within the scope, including their budgetary implications.

**8. Cross-functional responsibilities and contribution to the HR community:** o Contribute to the HR professional community, participate in sharing practices and lessons learned, and facilitate the circulation of relevant information between the scope, other cells, and headquarters. o Maintain working relationships with counterparts, other MSF sections, and stakeholders operating in the same contexts in order to promote alignment and the sharing of HR best practices. o Contribute, within the scope, to staff mobility, diversity, and gender balance, as well as to the recognition of career paths and expertise.

**Additional Activities:** o Contribute to the design and facilitation of HR training sessions. o Undertake short mission assignments to cover vacancies in coordination positions, according to operational needs.

## **Profile:**

**Experience:** Good knowledge of MSF, its organization, tools, and operational contexts. · At least 2 years of field experience (with MSF or another humanitarian NGO) in an HR coordination role. · Team management experience is mandatory. · Experience at OCP headquarters is an asset. · Training experience is an asset.

**Required Skills**: Knowledge of Human Resources Management techniques and tools (LIGO/Oracle/HRIS/HR Need, etc.). · Coaching and team support. · Interest in digital tools and applications (Office/Internet/SharePoint/etc.).

**Languages:** · English and French, minimum B2 level.

**Personal Attributes:** · Ability to cooperate, adapt, and work as part of a team. · Proactive, creative, and solution-oriented. · Strong dialogue and interpersonal skills. · Strong analytical and synthesis skills. · Organized, flexible, and autonomous. · Responsive, able to anticipate and manage priorities. · Willingness to travel to the field when required.

jobs.title: Public Health Medical Referent - Infectious Diseases (ID)
jobs.description:
**MSF is an international, independent medical humanitarian organization. We are a non-profit, self-governed worldwide movement of more than 63,000 people.**

**We provide emergency medical assistance during armed conflict, natural disasters, outbreaks of deadly diseases and assist those who are excluded from healthcare. MSF delivers care based on need and when we see injustice, we speak out. We are an organization that remains impartial, knowledgeable, and effective, and this is what makes the difference between life and death.**

**People are our priority. At Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF)/Artsen zonder Grenzen, we are committed to an inclusive culture that encourages and supports the diverse voices of our employees. We encourage diverse applicants including individuals of all gender identities, ages, sexual orientations, nationalities, races, religions, beliefs, social and marital status, people with different abilities and all other diversity characteristics and how they intersect.**

At the moment MSF-OCA is looking for a:

**Infectious Diseases (ID) Public Health Medical Referent - OCA Public Health Department**

The OCA Public Health Department is seeking an experienced Infectious Diseases professional to support clinicians working in Ebola Treatment Centres (ETCs) and other Viral Haemorrhagic Fever (VHF) contexts. The position focuses on strengthening the quality of patient care through technical support, coaching, mentoring, and field accompaniment of clinical teams.

**Main Responsibilities**

- Provide technical support, coaching, and mentoring to clinicians working in Ebola and other VHF contexts.
- Brief staff prior to deployment and provide ongoing remote and field-based support.
- Conduct regular field visits to strengthen clinical practice and quality of care.
- Support quality improvement initiatives through activities such as mortality reviews and rational prescription analysis.
- Strengthen systems and structures to improve quality of care in this and future VHF responses.
- Ensure clinical teams are guided by the latest best practice and evidence-based recommendations.
- Collaborate with relevant referents, including the current Infectious Diseases Advisors, to strengthen palliative care approaches.
- Act as a VHF technical resource for the Staff Health Unit regarding IMS and LHS Ebola-related health concerns.
- Analyze patient outcomes and programme data from OCA-run and OCA-supported treatment centres to identify opportunities for improving clinical care and patient pathways.
- Contribute to training and capacity-building initiatives for MSF and Ministry of Health staff.

**We are looking for a candidate who has:**

- Previous experience working in an Ebola response or other VHF context.
- Strong NGO field experience, preferably with MSF.
- Demonstrated experience of coaching and mentoring clinical teams.
- Strong analytical skills and the ability to translate clinical findings into improved patient care.
- Excellent collaboration and communication skills.
- A minimum French language level of C1.

**Deployment and Contract Conditions**

The position requires approximately 50-60% field deployment, with the remaining time dedicated to technical support, analysis, coordination, and mentoring activities.

Amsterdam or London are the preferred duty stations. Nairobi and Berlin may also consider suitable candidates. Flexibility regarding headquarters presence may be required depending on operational, travel, visa or quarantine constraints.

Please note: Accommodation is provided during field deployments only. Candidates are responsible for arranging and funding their own accommodation at their duty station when not deployed.

The anticipated start date is as soon as possible. The initial contract duration is 6 months, with the possibility of a 6-month extension.

**Information and Application**

If you recognise yourself in this profile and meet the requirements, we encourage you to apply directly via the Apply button on this page and upload the following documents:

- Your most recent CV
- A cover letter explaining your motivation to work with MSF

Deadline for applications: December 1st, 23:59 CET.

jobs.title: Terms of References (ToR) for a Consultancy to Conduct a Feasibility Study for the proposed project: A Voice for Inclusion.
jobs.description:
**Terms of References (ToR) for a Consultancy to Conduct a Feasibility Study for the proposed project: A Voice for Inclusion – Equal Education and a Strong Civil Society for Children with Disabilities in Ethiopia, The Gambia and Zambia.**

Assignment period: December 2026 – January 2027

- Location:Ethiopia, The Gambia and Zambia
- Commissioned by:ChildFund
- Main Partners: ChildFund Deutschland, ChildFund Ethiopia, ChildFund The Gambia, ChildFund Zambia, Tesfa Birhan, Saama Kairo Federation, Chibombo/Mumbwa Child Development Agency, Kafue Child Development Agency
- Donor: Project to be submitted to BMZ

## **Background and Context**

### Context of the assignment

Despite the ratification of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD) by Ethiopia (in 2010), The Gambia (in 2015) and Zambia (in 2010), many children with disabilities continue to face significant barriers to accessing and successfully completing primary education. Children with severe or multiple disabilities, intellectual or learning disabilities, sensory impairments, and disabilities that remain unidentified are often among the most excluded. Exclusion is further compounded by factors such as gender, age, poverty and geographical remoteness. In addition, the absence of systematic processes for identifying children with disabilities frequently limits their access to appropriate support services, accommodations and referral mechanisms.

Preliminary problem analyses conducted in all three countries suggest a number of common barriers and root causes. At family and community level, these include poverty and disability-related costs, transport and distance barriers, limited awareness of available support services, stigma and discrimination, weak parent support structures, safety concerns, and low expectations regarding the educational potential of children with disabilities. At school level, challenges include inadequate teacher preparation for inclusive education, insufficient follow-up coaching and mentoring, limited availability of assistive devices and adapted learning materials, inaccessible infrastructure, overcrowded classrooms, and constrained institutional and financial resources. Across all three countries, gaps are also evident between national policy commitments and their implementation at district, community and school levels. Common issues include weak coordination between sectors and administrative levels, insufficient funding, limited use of disability-disaggregated data, weak referral systems, and limited opportunities for meaningful participation of children with disabilities and their caregivers in planning and decision-making processes.

In Zambia, UNCRPD commitments are domesticated through the Persons with Disabilities Act No. 6 of 2012, which provides for the right to inclusive education and established the Zambia Agency for Persons with Disabilities (ZAPD), alongside the Education Act of 2011 and the Children’s Code Act of 2022. The free education policy introduced in 2022 removed school fees, yet children with disabilities in rural and peri-urban districts such as Kafue, Mumbwa and Chibombo continue to face barriers that fee removal alone does not address, including distance to school, limited district-level assessment and specialised services, few teachers trained in inclusive or special education, and stigma.

In The Gambia, commitments under the UNCRPD are supported by the Disability Act (2021), the Children’s Act, and the Ministry of Basic and Secondary Education’s Inclusive Education Policy Framework. Despite these policy commitments, children with disabilities continue to face significant barriers to accessing quality education, including late identification of disabilities, limited availability of specialised assessment and support services, inadequate assistive and learning resources, social stigma, and insufficient capacity within mainstream schools to respond to diverse learning needs. These challenges are often more pronounced in rural and underserved communities.

In Ethiopia, commitments to inclusive education are operationalised through the Constitution (Article 41), the education policy framework, and the current Special Needs/Inclusive Education Strategy (2022/23-2029/30), which aims to ensure equitable access to quality education for children, youth and adults with special educational needs and disabilities. Despite this strong policy commitment, significant barriers continue to hinder implementation at federal, regional, woreda and school levels, including weak disability data systems, limited early identification and referral mechanisms, shortages of trained inclusive education professionals, inadequate assistive devices and adapted learning materials, inaccessible infrastructure, and persistent stigma. These challenges are often compounded by poverty, displacement, geographical isolation and gender-related disadvantages, particularly in rural, pastoralist, conflict-affected and underserved communities.

While the analyses point to significant similarities in the patterns of exclusion across Ethiopia, The Gambia and Zambia, they are also highlighting important contextual differences. This creates opportunities for structured cross-country learning, knowledge exchange and the adaptation of effective approaches across different contexts. The planned project aims to address these challenges with an integrated micro-meso-macro approach: communities and families are sensitized and empowered; schools are developed into inclusive learning environments, mainly through training and development plans; and civil society organisations are strengthened to carry out advocacy work for inclusive education. The multi-country nature of the program offers an opportunity to generate evidence, promote cross-learning and identify scalable approaches that can strengthen inclusive education systems beyond the targeted locations.

Inclusive education is both a rights-based obligation and a strategic investment in human capital, social inclusion and sustainable development. Ensuring that children with disabilities can access and succeed in education contributes to national development priorities, advances SDG 4 commitments, and supports broader efforts to ensure that no child is left behind.

### Brief about ChildFund International as the organization commissioning the study

ChildFund International is a global child- and youth-focused development and humanitarian organization dedicated to advancing the well-being, resilience, and rights of children and young people, particularly those facing vulnerability and exclusion. Working through local partners, communities, governments, and civil society, ChildFund promotes locally led and owned development approaches that strengthen systems, build community capacity, and create sustainable impact for children and their families. Its programmes focus on education, child protection, health, livelihoods, and youth empowerment, with an emphasis on achieving lasting outcomes that enable children and young people to learn, thrive, and contribute meaningfully to their communities.

This assignment is commissioned by ChildFund International to inform the design and implementation of a multi-country inclusive education programme in Ethiopia, The Gambia, and Zambia. The International Office (IO) will provide overall strategic direction, technical leadership, and quality assurance; the Africa Regional Office (RO) will provide regional coordination, technical oversight, and facilitate cross-country learning; while the respective Country Offices (COs) will lead country-level coordination, stakeholder engagement, and contextual guidance to ensure the study reflects national priorities and local realities.

### **Brief about the proposed project**

The proposed multi-country programme seeks to improve equitable access to, participation in, and quality of inclusive primary education for children with disabilities in Ethiopia, The Gambia, and Zambia. The programme is founded on the recognition that educational exclusion results from interconnected barriers at household, community, school, and systems levels, requiring a coordinated and multi-level response.

Through a locally grounded and systems-strengthening approach, the programme aims to ensure that children with disabilities, including those who are currently out of school, are identified, enrolled, actively engaged in learning, and able to make measurable progress in foundational literacy and numeracy. Particular attention will be given to children facing multiple and intersecting forms of exclusion, including girls with disabilities, children with high support needs, children living in poverty, and those in remote or underserved areas.

To achieve these outcomes, the programme will pursue an integrated micro-meso-macro approach that combines community engagement, inclusive school development, institutional capacity strengthening, and policy engagement through four complementary result areas.

**Proposed Output 1: Family and Community Environment**

Children with disabilities will be identified through community-based identification and referral mechanisms. Parents/caregivers will be supported to promote school enrolment and effectively address the learning needs of children with disabilities, including through effective referral systems and linkages to service providers, in line with the programme's systems-strengthening and sustainability objectives. Parents/caregiver self-help groups will be established and/or strengthened to address barriers to education and support sustained participation, retention, and educational success for children with disabilities.

**Proposed Output 2: Inclusive Schools and Learning Environments**

Target schools will be supported to strengthen inclusive teaching and learning practices through teacher training, coaching and mentoring and the development of learning materials and methods aligned with the needs of children with disabilities. Existing school structures will be trained and supported to introduce inclusive school development plans, thereby embedding inclusive practices within school systems and leadership structures to support long-term implementation, ownership, and scalability beyond the life of the programme. Model schools will be equipped with accessible infrastructure, demonstrating how accessible learning environments contribute to sustainable institutional change and improved learning outcomes; while other project schools will be supported to identify, prioritise and cost accessibility improvements, with project funding complementing local resources and budgets where available.

**Proposed Output 3: Civil Society Capacity and Advocacy**

Through cross-national learning and collaboration, civil society organisations will strengthen their capacity to generate and use evidence on effective and cost-efficient inclusive education practices, engage in evidence-based advocacy, and promote the active participation of persons with disabilities and their representatives in education policy processes. A joint cross-national platform will facilitate the long-term exchange of evidence, implementation experiences, costing data and advocacy tools to support the institutionalisation and financing of inclusive education practices.

**Proposed Output 4: Policy Implementation and Local Adoption**

Under Output 4, civil society organisations and OPDs will be supported to translate evidence and lessons learned from project implementation and cross-country exchange into advocacy messages, policy recommendations and budget proposals for inclusive education. Through engagement with policy-makers, planning bodies and coordination mechanisms, opportunities will be created to foster government ownership and to promote the uptake of effective and cost-efficient inclusive education practices within planning, budgeting and resource allocation processes. This will support the use of evidence to inform scalable and sustainable system-level improvements, strengthen the institutionalisation of inclusive education practices within government systems, and contribute to the sustained delivery of inclusive education services beyond the project period.

Through these interconnected interventions, the programme aims to contribute to a situation in which children with disabilities in the target communities are able to enrol in school, participate effectively in classroom learning and achieve measurable improvements in foundational literacy and numeracy. In the longer term, the programme seeks to strengthen inclusive education systems and support the sustainable implementation of inclusive education policies and practices across the three participating countries.

- ## Purpose and Scope of the Feasibility Study

### Study Type

A feasibility study provides an evidence-based foundation for project design and investment decisions by assessing implementation readiness, opportunities, risks, and key assumptions and offering guidance and possible improvements. The findings will inform programme optimisation and effectiveness, identify pathways for sustainable and scalable impact, and help ensure that resources are directed towards interventions with the greatest potential to improve inclusive education outcomes.

### Purpose of the Study

The purpose of the feasibility study is particularly to assess the feasibility of the proposed project and systematically examine the extent to which the project approach can plausibly achieve the planned changes under the existing conditions. Specifically, the study focuses on these specific topics:

**1. Evidence Base and Context Analysis**

- Identify and review relevant international, regional and national evidence related to disability-inclusive primary education, including successful approaches, lessons learned, policy frameworks, implementation models and emerging good practices.
- Establish baseline information on the current situation of children with disabilities, schools, communities and relevant stakeholders in the target areas in order to inform project design and future monitoring. All proposed baseline data should be disaggregated by region/district, sex, age, grade/educational level and type of disability.
- Map existing systems, services, structures and coordination mechanisms relevant to disability-inclusive education and determine where the project should strengthen existing systems, fill critical gaps or avoid duplication of existing initiatives.

**2. Relevance and Strategic Fit**

- Evaluate the relevance of the proposed project activities, objectives and strategies in relation to the needs of target groups, existing systems and the broader context.
- Assess the strategic rationale and expected added value of the proposed multi-country approach compared to separate country-level interventions. The study should analyse common challenges, complementary strengths, opportunities for cross-country learning, joint advocacy, knowledge exchange, mutual capacity development and the transfer of effective inclusive education practices, as well as factors that justify the selection of Ethiopia, The Gambia and Zambia as participating countries.
- Recommend practical and financially realistic strategies for ensuring that the project benefits children with different types of disabilities, including those who are often most excluded, such as children with intellectual disabilities, communication difficulties, multiple disabilities and higher support needs.

**3. Validation of the Proposed Intervention**

- Validate the project's Theory of Change, he proposed indicators, baseline and target values and recommend revisions where necessary to ensure realistic and measurable results; also assess the plausibility of the proposed causal pathways and expected outcomes.
- Assess how the proposed intervention can most effectively contribute to meaningful participation and measurable improvements in foundational literacy and numeracy outcomes for children with disabilities. The study should identify critical success factors, potential barriers and additional measures required to ensure that increased enrolment and attendance translate into improved learning outcomes.
- Assess the availability and capacity of existing systems for feasible, ethically appropriate, disability-responsive assessment, identification, referral and learning support/educational-support pathways, referral completion, feedback loops, case follow-up and service-capacity constraints. This should include an analysis of whether learning assessments can be adapted to different impairments, the uptake of Universal Design for Learning in the target schools so far, the availability of specialised teaching and learning materials and assistive devices, and the capacity of government services, OPDs and other actors to assess children's needs and facilitate access to appropriate support.
- Test key assumptions underlying the project design, including assumptions related to identification and referral systems, teacher retention, stakeholder engagement, service availability, maintenance of infrastructure, the added value of cross-country learning and the sustainability of project-supported approaches.
- Assess the feasibility of local adoption and financing of tested inclusive education practices by schools, local authorities and government structures, including opportunities for incorporation into existing planning, budgeting, supervision and school improvement systems
- Assess the integration of cross-cutting issues, including gender equality, child safeguarding, conflict sensitivity and environmental sustainability.

**4. Capacity and Feasibility Assessment**

- Assess the operational feasibility of the proposed intervention, including availability of resources, institutional arrangements and stakeholder commitment at community, district and national levels.
- Assess the organisational and technical capacities of the proposed implementing partners and evaluate whether the proposed intervention is realistic and proportionate to their current capacities. The study should identify existing strengths, capacity gaps and the capacity development measures required to enable partners to successfully implement, monitor and sustain the proposed interventions.
- Identify external factors, contextual influences and implementation risks that may affect the achievement and sustainability of project results.
- Assess the likelihood that project-supported approaches, services and practices can be sustained, institutionalised and financed by local actors after project completion.

**5. Optimisation and Recommendations**

- Assess the extent to which the proposed project design is realistic within the available budget and identify opportunities for simplification, prioritisation and cost-efficiency.
- Review and, where necessary, refine the proposed intervention strategy, impact matrix, outputs and indicators (including baseline and target values) based on study findings, including the development of recommendations for indicators and targets that have not yet been defined.
- Provide evidence-based recommendations for improving project design, implementation arrangements, targeting, monitoring, partnership development, capacity strengthening, sustainability and scalability

### Assessment Criteria

The study should present the context of the planned project at all relevant levels (micro, meso, macro) and also include key data relevant to the project regarding the initial situation. Building on this, an analysis should be carried out to determine the extent to which the chosen approach can contribute to resolving the problem for the target groups and other stakeholders. Recommendations for adjustments to the specific project concept – including the draft impact matrix and suggested measures – should be formulated in as concrete a manner as possible. In doing so, consideration must be given to the actors and stakeholders to be involved, proposals for areas to be monitored in terms of outcome and impact measurement, and the opportunities and risks involved.

Furthermore, the proposed project should be critically assessed in the light of the OECD DAC criteria of relevance, coherence, effectiveness, efficiency, impact and sustainability:

1. **Relevance:** Does the planned project approach address a key development issue or a critical development bottleneck in the partner countries? Are the focus, priorities and objectives (approach) of the planned project aligned with the target groups and clearly defined? To what extent do the intervention objectives and design adequately take into account the specific needs of the target groups and structural barriers in the project countries, the partner organisations, and the political programmes? Are the norms and standards of the approach compatible with those of the target groups? Is the project designed with conflict sensitivity in mind (the ‘Do No Harm’ principle)?
2. **Coherence:** To what extent are the planned activities consistent with human rights principles (inclusion, participation), conventions and relevant standards/guidelines? To what extent are there synergies and links between the planned project and other interventions by the same partners and other actors? What overlaps or common ground exist between the target groups of this project and those of other actors’ projects in the same context? To what extent does the intervention add value and avoid duplication of effort?
3. **Effectiveness:** Are the causal relationships (including assumptions) plausible? What negative effects might arise? Is the chosen methodological approach appropriate to the context and sufficient to achieve the project’s objective? At what level (multi-level approach) should additional measures be planned to increase effectiveness? How will changes be measured (baseline and endline tools)? Are the indicators in the draft impact matrix suited for this?
4. **Efficiency:** To what extent can the planned measures be implemented within the planned timeframe and allocated funds? Which staffing investments, operating costs and staffing levels are recommended proportionate to the intended objectives?
5. **Impact:** How does the project objective (outcome) contribute specifically to the overarching objective (impact)? To what extent does the planned project contribute to structural development, serve as a model and have a broad, cross-national impact beyond progress within each country and beyond the project period? At what levels are standards or structures being changed?
6. **Sustainability:** How can the sustainability of the results and impacts be ensured and strengthened (structurally, economically, socially, environmentally)? What long-term capacities are being built up within the target group to enable them to continue the implemented measures independently? What positive changes (role behaviour, mechanisms, networks and others) benefit civil society in the long term? What personnel risks for those implementing the measures, as well as institutional and contextual risks, affect sustainability, and how can these be minimised?

On the basis of the key findings relating to the purpose of the study and the assessment of the project concept against the DAC criteria, the study should make clear **recommendations** which specific proposals and improvements should be incorporated into the project concept.

### Key assessment questions

Building on the specific topics described above and the OECD-DAC criteria described, the study should address the following key questions:

**1. Purpose and use of the feasibility study**

- How conducive is the context (sector, components, project regions) with regard to the projects’ objective?
- How feasible is achieving the proposed project outcome and the underlying Theory of Change as well as the proposed indicators? And how coherent is the proposed intervention across sectors, outputs and countries? Which critical assumptions underpin the project's Theory of Change, and to what extent are these assumptions supported by available evidence and stakeholder perspectives?
- Which factors are most likely to influence whether increased enrolment and attendance translate into improved learning outcomes for children with disabilities?
- How can the study findings contribute to adaptive management, organisational learning and project refinement across all three countries?

**2. Methodology**

- What participatory methods, tools, and resources will be used for data collection and analysis (incl. recommendation of baseline and endline tools)?
- Which stakeholders will be involved? What are their backgrounds and interests? How can meaningful participation of children with disabilities, caregivers, schools, civil society organisations, OPDs and government stakeholders be ensured?

**3. Initial situation and problem analysis, on macro- meso- and micro-levels**

- What current problems of children with disabilities have been identified at micro, meso and macro levels, relevant to the proposed project? Which of the causes of these problems will be prioritised and addressed in the project?
- What existing root causes, local potential, structures (institutions, networks, umbrella organizations etc.) and social mechanisms can be built on? What gaps have been identified in the system? Which existing identification, referral, assessment and support systems for children with disabilities are functioning effectively and where do significant gaps remain?
- What specialised teaching and learning materials, assistive devices and support services are currently available, and where are the most significant gaps? To what extent can existing education assessment systems be adapted to different impairment groups, and what constraints currently limit equitable assessment of learning outcomes?
- What currently prevents children with disabilities from progressing from enrolment to meaningful participation and improvements in foundational literacy and numeracy?
- Are there any approaches or results from previous development measures? If yes, how can they be extended?
- Which existing government, community and OPD structures should be strengthened rather than duplicated by the project?
- What other circumstances, for example conflict dynamics, must be taken into account in the context of the selected countries?

**4. Local project partners in the partner countries**

- Which organisations have been selected as local project partners, and why? How will the local project partners’ ownership be improved?
- Are the partners’ resources and strengths, both individually and at an organisational level, well understood? To what extent does the project planning align with the current capacities of the local partners Tesfa Birhan, Saama Kairo Federation, Chibombo/Mumbwa Child Development Agency, Kafue Child Development Agency? Is selective support from staff of the ChildFund International Country Offices necessary and justified and which project functions can realistically be led by the local partners themselves?
- What coordination structure between the local partners is recommended?
- What relevant technical, methodological and advocacy competencies will be further developed within the local partners through the project to strengthen their long-term capacity for implementation, coordination and advocacy?

**5. Beneficiaries and other stakeholders (on a micro-, meso- and macro-level)**

- How (with which criteria) will the direct beneficiaries be selected, and by whom?
- Which groups of children with disabilities are most likely to benefit from the proposed intervention as currently designed, and which groups may require adapted approaches or additional support measures?
- How is the diversity within the target groups, including disability type, age, gender, socio-economic situation and location, and to what extent must the project take this into account? How can different disability groups can be meaningfully included and the proposed interventions be adapted to address the specific needs of different impairment groups and support requirements?
- What potential do the beneficiaries have for self-help?
- Do the beneficiaries and other stakeholders have a common understanding of the problems, prioritising process and objectives of the project? Do the interests of other stakeholders align? Do any conflicts of interest exist?
- How strong is the various stakeholders’ support for the project, for example, in terms of their own contribution? In what ways might they influence the project?

**6. Multi-Country Dimension**

- What is the added value of implementing the proposed project with a multi-country approach compared to stand-alone country projects? What common objective – beyond progress within each country – justifies the multi-country approach? Does this justify the additional complexity and coordination effort of a three-country programme?
- What is the rationale for the selection of Ethiopia, The Gambia and Zambia? What are the relationships between the three project countries and what are shared and country-specific barriers, opportunities for cross-country learning and potential for joint advocacy and knowledge exchange? Could a project with only two countries achieve similar results more effectively?
- What existing (cross-national) structures does the project build upon, and what will remain after the project ends? How can sustainability be ensured across all three countries, and into which umbrella organization, active in all three countries, can results of the project be incorporated; and what lasting mechanisms for cooperation, joint learning and advocacy could be established or strengthened?

**7. Strategic and Financial Feasibility**

- How realistic is the proposed intervention design under the available budget envelope?
- Are any adjustments required to the indicators, baseline and target values to ensure they are achievable, measurable and aligned with the proposed intervention design and budget?
- What are potential simplifications and prioritization options, and which project components are essential to preserve the intended outcomes and Theory of Change?
- Which elements of the proposed intervention are most likely to be institutionalised and financed by local actors after project completion, and what mechanisms or arrangements are required to sustain both project results and cross-country cooperation beyond external funding?

## Study Methodology

The study will comprise both desk-based research and fieldwork. It will involve a combination of primary data collection and secondary data review.

Selected secondary data sources will be made available to the contractor. The following documents will be provided:

- Initial concept note for the planned project
- Draft impact matrix
- Draft theory of change
- Initial problem analysis conducted by the partners
- Partner documents relevant to the planned project
- Selected national strategy documents, background papers, references

For the collection of primary data, the contractor is encouraged to propose appropriate methodological approaches (quantitative, qualitative, or mixed methods). The study methodology should, where appropriate and ethically feasible, include the direct participation of the project’s primary target group – children with disabilities. The study should ensure that the voices and perspectives of children with disabilities and their families are reflected in the findings, particularly with regard to their participation in project activities and perceived changes in their living conditions.

The contractor is expected to propose appropriate, age-sensitive, and ethically sound data collection methods for engaging with children and youths, in line with relevant safeguarding and ethical standards.

In addition, the study should include the following data collection methodologies:

- Desk and literature review
- Stakeholder consultations
- Field visits
- Key Informant Interviews with partner staff, community leaders, and other relevant stakeholders
- Focus Group Discussions with intended target groups
- Household or individual surveys (quantitative data collection)
- Workshop/validation meeting to review preliminary findings with partners and stakeholders

## Ethical Consideration

It is essential to ensure that the risks of potential harm to participants arising from the data collection process are minimized and clearly outweighed by the potential benefits of the study’s outcomes. The contractor must address critical ethical issues in the design and implementation of the study, ensuring that the rights, safety, and confidentiality of all information providers are fully protected. Key considerations include, but are not limited to:

**Compliance** with legal and regulatory requirements, including permissions for data collection, storage, export, and, where applicable, interviewing or collecting information about children and youth.

- **For Zambia:** Research ethics clearance from the Research Ethics Committee, and authorisation from the National Health Research Authority (NHRA) where health-related data (e.g., functional screening) are collected; written authority from the Ministry of Education and the respective DEBS offices to conduct research in schools; and compliance with the Data Protection Act No. 3 of 2021 and the Children’s Code Act of 2022.
- **For The Gambia**: IRB approval from the university of the Gambia (UTG), Compliance with national child protection and safeguarding regulations, relevant data protection requirements, approvals from MoBSE and Regional Education Directorates, and adherence to ChildFund safeguarding standards when engaging children with disabilities and their caregivers.
- **For Ethiopa**: Determine whether ethics review is required, secure federal/regional/woreda and school permissions, and comply with Personal Data Protection Proclamation No. 1321/2024, including special protections for children, disability/health data, storage and cross-border transfer
- Measures to ensure the secure storage and management of collected data.
- Protocols to maintain anonymity and confidentiality of participants.
- Ensuring that participation is voluntary and based on informed consent.
- Safeguarding the rights and welfare of participants and the communities involved.

The contractor should take all reasonable steps to ensure that the study is designed and conducted to:

- Respect and protect the rights, dignity, and welfare of all participants.
- Produce technically accurate, reliable, and valid findings.
- Conduct the study in a transparent, impartial, and accountable manner.
- Contribute to organizational learning and accountability.

Ethical considerations must be an integral part of the study process at all stages to maintain the highest standards of professional conduct.

## Time Schedule and Deliverables

The study will be carried out according to the following timeline and corresponding tasks:

**Timeline Tasks**

- 1st week of December 2026- Briefing and preparation
- 2nd week of December- Desk review and preparation of the inception report
- 2nd week of December- Review of inception report by the project team
- 3rd week of December - Finalization of the inception report
- 3rd and 4th week of December- Development of data collection tools
- 1st week of January- Primary data collection and Field visit(s)
- 2nd week of January-Data analysis
- 3rd week of January-Drafting of the preliminary study report and Presentation of preliminary findings / validation workshop
- 4th week of January-Review of draft preliminary study report by the project team
- End of January 2027-Finalization of the study report and final submission

Each deliverable is expected to be submitted according to the agreed timeline, ensuring sufficient time for review and feedback from the project team. Specific dates for each activity and deliverable will be defined in consultation with the contractor and the project team and documented in the inception report.

### Deliverables

- **Inception Report:**
The contractor should prepare an inception report before commencing the full data collection exercise. The report should detail the contractor’s understanding of the planned project and the study, explaining how each question will be addressed through proposed methods, data sources, and data collection procedures. It should also include a proposed schedule of tasks, activities, and deliverables.
- **Preliminary Study Report:**
The contractor should provide a concise report presenting all preliminary findings, conclusions, and recommendations. The methodology used should also be described.
- **PowerPoint Presentation of Key Findings:**
The main findings from the preliminary report should be presented by the contractor during the validation workshop.

**Final Study Report:**
The final report should be aligned with the Sample outline for evaluation reports from donor (which will be provided to the contractor) and include, among others:

- Executive summary
- Description of the planned project
- Study goals and objectives
- Study methodology and data collection tools used
- Presentation of main findings and conclusions
- Country-specific chapters or annexes for Ethiopia, The Gambia and Zambia, each containing a country context analysis, partner capacity assessment and country-level recommendations
- Overall recommendations; executive decision matrix showing issue, evidence, recommendation, priority, cost implication, responsible actor and proposed revision to the concept/logframe
- Annexes, including data collection tools, list of interviewees, sources, and other relevant documentation

All documents, except annexes to the feasibility study report, must be submitted in English. The report should have a maximum of 30 pages (except annexes).

## Expertise Profile of the Study Team

The study will be conducted by a lead consultant with proven experience in conducting feasibility studies for development projects and sectorial expertise in inclusive education, supported by qualified local consultants in the three countries.

A statement on the independence of the study team from the organizations involved is mandatory.

The consultant(s) we are seeking should meet the following criteria:

- **Professional experience:** Minimum of 5 years of experience in evaluating development projects and assessing the feasibility of planned development projects. Evidence of this experience should be provided.
- **Technical expertise:** Demonstrated knowledge of relevant study methods and tools as well as education and inclusion programs in international development coordination.
- **Stakeholder engagement:** Experience with participatory approaches, stakeholder consultation, and transparent knowledge management.
- **Methodological, analytical and communication skills:** Strong analytical, report writing, and presentation skills.
- **Language proficiency:** Fluent in English (mandatory), fluency in relevant local languages in Ethiopia, The Gambia and Zambia required for local consultants
- **Formal:** Permit/Ability to work in Ethiopia, The Gambia and Zambia

## Management and Coordination of the Study

The Regional Office (RO) will provide overall leadership and coordination of the study, including the procurement and management of the lead consultant responsible for implementing the assignment across the three countries. The lead consultant will oversee the study's implementation, engage qualified local consultants to conduct country-level data collection and analysis, and prepare individual country reports. Building on these findings, the lead consultant will synthesize the country reports into a single regional study report for submission to the Regional Office. The RO will review and finalize the report and formally submit the final study report to ChildFund Deutschland. Throughout the process, close collaboration and consultation will be maintained with ChildFund Deutschland to ensure alignment with the study objectives, methodology, quality standards, and expected deliverables.

## Evaluation Criteria

Proposals will be assessed by an evaluation panel. The technical proposal accounts for 70% (70 points) and the financial proposal for 30% (30 points) of the total score of 100 points. Financial proposals will only be opened for bidders whose technical proposals achieve a minimum of 49 out of 70 points (70% of the technical score).

## 8.1. Technical evaluation (70 points)

**Criterion**

**Description**

1\. Understanding of the assignment and methodological approach- **15 Marks**

Understanding of the ToR and of the inclusive education context in Ethiopia, The Gambia and Zambia; rigour and feasibility of the mixed-methods design, sampling, tools and analysis plan; coverage of the OECD DAC criteria and key assessment questions; approach to validating the Theory of Change, indicators and baseline/target values and to producing prioritised recommendations.

2\. Participation, ethics and safeguarding- **10 Marks**

Approach to the meaningful and ethical participation of children with disabilities, caregivers and OPDs; child safeguarding, informed consent, data protection and country-specific ethical clearance.

3.Team composition- **15 Marks**

The lead/principal consultant MUST have associates within the participating countries (Ethiopia, Zambia and The Gambia) or structures to bring them onboard within a very short turnaround time.

4\. Qualifications and experience of the study team- **10 Marks**

Lead consultant with at least 5 years of experience in evaluating and assessing the feasibility of development projects; expertise in inclusive education and disability inclusion; equally qualified local consultants with relevant languages and permits in all three countries; complementary skills and gender balance.

5\. Past performance and references- **10 Marks**

Two comparable feasibility studies or evaluations (preferably for BMZ or similar donors, in Africa, in education or disability inclusion) with report samples, and at least two client references.

6\. Work plan, risk management and independence- **10 Marks**

Realistic work plan aligned with Section 5 and cross-country coordination; risk mitigation and quality assurance for country and synthesis reports; statement of independence and conflict-of-interest disclosure.

**Total technical score- 70 Marks**

7\. **Financial evaluation (30 points)**

The financial proposal must present a transparent budget in a single currency, with professional fees (daily rates and number of days) for the lead and local consultants, travel and logistics for field visits in the three countries, data collection costs, and applicable taxes. The budget must be realistic and consistent with the proposed methodology and work plan

## Schedule of Payment

Payment will be made in three instalments against approved deliverables, as set out below. Percentages refer to the total contract value agreed in the contract.

- **Instalment 1-** Inception report approved by ChildFund at End of 2nd week of December 2026- 30%
- **Instalment 2**- Preliminary study report and validation workshop completed- End of 4th week of January 2027- 30%
- **Instalment 3**- Final study report (including country chapters and executive decision matrix) approved by ChildFund -End of January 2027- 40%

**Total- 100%**

## Required Documents

Consultant should submit the documents as mentioned below along with the Technical and Financial proposal.

- Certificate of Incorporation / Business Registration Certificate
- CR12 (where applicable)
- Valid Tax Compliance Certificate
- Updated Company Profile
- Bank details
- Key contact details (Contact Person, Postal Address, Telephone and Email address)

**Annex 1: Country-specific guidance and questions for the study**

- ***Country- Zambia***

**Regarding Evidence Base and Context Analysis**

1. baseline data should draw on Ministry of Education EMIS / Annual School Census data for the target schools
2. The mapping of existing systems, services, structures and coordination mechanisms should include, among others: the Ministry of Education (directorate responsible for special/inclusive education, Provincial Education Offices, DEBS offices and Zonal Resource Centres); ZAPD; the Ministry of Community Development and Social Services (social welfare, Social Cash Transfer); the Ministry of Health (early identification and rehabilitation services); the Zambia Institute of Special Education (ZAMISE); OPDs affiliated to the Zambia Federation of Disability Organisations (ZAFOD); the Zambia National Education Coalition (ZANEC); and NGOs active in inclusive education in the three districts.

**Regarding the Validation of the Proposed Intervention**
